summary: A standards-track document defining two ways to store lookup information in an X.500 directory, using a subtree of entries: mapping a key to one or more values, and mapping a distinguished name to values that the entry's owner does not define. It replaces RFC 1837.

eli5.summary: Think of a phone book that can also hold little lookup lists, like a dictionary. This memo explains how to build such lookup lists inside a big directory of names.

questions: how to represent tables in x.500
how to store a lookup table in x.500
what is a distinguished name table entry
subtitle: Two simple patterns for keeping lookup tables and private subtrees inside an X.500 directory.

tldr.problem: Applications such as X.400 mail routing need to store key-to-value lookups and local information about globally named objects in the X.500 Directory, where the key often has no global name.
tldr.mechanism: A table is a single-level subtree under a Table entry, with one entry per key. A subtree is a private root under which entries are named by distinguished names relative to that root.
tldr.outcome: The techniques were built for MHS use of the Directory but are specified separately because they apply more widely. RFC 2293 obsoletes RFC 1837.

today: RFC 2293 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 1837.

sections.title: Two Kinds of Lookup Information
sections.content:
RFC 2293 defines techniques for representing two kinds of information mapping in the OSI Directory (X.500). The first maps a key to a value or set of values, as in a table lookup. The second maps a distinguished name to an associated value or values, where the values are not defined by the owner of the entry. The second is achieved with a directory subtree.

The techniques were developed to support MHS (message handling system) use of the Directory, but the RFC specifies them separately because they have more general applicability. It obsoletes RFC 1837.
sections.eli5: The memo gives two recipes for storing lookup lists in a big directory. One is for looking up a word, and one is for adding your own notes to someone else's entry.

sections.title: Representing Flat Tables
sections.content:
A table is an unordered set of key-to-value mappings, used when the key cannot be represented as a global name. The RFC gives four reasons: the object has no natural global name; it can only be named effectively as the key to a binding; it has a global name but the table holds parameters that cannot go in its global entry; or information is grouped as a performance optimization so the block can be widely replicated.

Parameters might not go in the global entry because the object has no directory entry, there is no authority to place them there, or they only make sense in the context of the table.

A table is a single level subtree. Its root is an entry of object class table, named with a descriptive common name. The table is located where it fits its function: below the MTA's entry if private to an MTA, or under the organization if shared by the organization's MTAs.
sections.eli5: A table is like a labelled shoebox of index cards. The box has a name, and each card inside holds one key and its answer.

sections.title: Table Entry Classes
sections.content:
The generic table entry contains only a description. Every instance is subclassed, and the subclass defines the naming attribute. Two subclasses are defined.

  • textTableEntry has a mandatory textTableKey and an optional textTableValue. It suits text keys that map to single or multiple values of any type, and supports the common text-to-text mapping. Additional values may be defined.
  • distinguishedNameTableEntry has a mandatory distinguishedNameTableKey and is used to associate information with globally defined objects. No value attributes are defined; an application makes appropriate subtyping to define the values it needs.

The distinguished name approach should be used when the number of objects in the table is small or very sparsely spread over the DIT. When there are many objects, or they are tightly clustered, the subtree approach is preferable.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of index card. One has a plain word on it. The other has a full address of something already in the book, so you can add notes about it.

sections.title: Table Examples
sections.content:
The RFC's first example, which it calls fictitious, takes an MTA named CN=Bells, OU=Computer Science, O=University College London, C=GB. A table named CN=domain-nicknames sits below it. To map "euclid" to "bloomsbury.ac.uk", an entry with TextTableKey=euclid in that table holds the attribute TextTableValue=bloomsbury.ac.uk.

The second example uses distinguishedNameTableEntry. A table CN=MTA Bilateral Agreements below the same MTA maps MTA names to bilateral agreement information. The relative distinguished name of each entry is the distinguished name of the MTA it describes, such as CN=Q3T21, ADMD=Gold 400, C=GB, and the bilateral information is an attribute of that entry.
sections.eli5: One example maps a nickname to a real computer name. The other keeps a note about another mail computer, filed under that computer's full address.

sections.title: Representing Subtrees
sections.content:
A subtree is similar to a table, except that keys are constructed as a distinguished name hierarchy relative to the subtree's location in the DIT. The subtree effectively starts a private "root" and names things relative to it. Typically it associates local information with global objects. Functionally it is equivalent to a table with distinguished name keys: the table approach is best when the tree is very sparse, and the subtree approach suits more populated trees.

The subtree object class defines the root, analogously to the table, with a mandatory common name and an optional manager. Entries inside generally use the same definitions as the global object, so no specific object classes for subtree entries are needed.

Example: University College London (O=University College London, C=GB) has a CN=private subtree below it. UCL-specific information on Inria is stored in O=Inria, C=FR, CN=private subtree, O=University College London, C=GB.
sections.eli5: A subtree is like your own private copy of part of a map, where you can scribble notes next to places without changing the real map.

sections.title: Security and Object Identifiers
sections.content:
The security section says only that security considerations are not discussed in this memo.

An appendix assigns object identifiers under the Isode consortium's mhs-ds arc for the five object classes (subtree, table, tableEntry, textTableEntry, distinguishedNameTableEntry) and the three attributes (textTableKey, textTableValue, distinguishedNameTableKey). Practical examples of the mapping, and the acknowledgments, are in RFC 1801.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about safety. It does hand out unique ID numbers so every piece has its own name tag.

references.text: Kille, S.E., "X.400-MHS use of the X.500 directory to support X.400-MHS routing," RFC 1801, June 1995.
